reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO & national toxicology guidance
clinicalPearls: Alkalis typically cause liquefactive necrosis with deep, penetrating oesophageal injury, whereas acids cause coagulative necrosis that more often damages the stomach
The absence of visible oral or oropharyngeal burns does not exclude significant oesophageal or gastric injury
Early features include drooling, odynophagia, dysphagia, retrosternal or epigastric pain, and stridor if the airway is involved
Do not induce emesis, give neutralising agents, or attempt gastric lavage, as these can worsen tissue injury and increase the risk of perforation and aspiration
Activated charcoal is not useful and obscures endoscopic assessment, so it should be avoided
Early upper GI endoscopy (usually within the first day, once the patient is stable) is used to grade injury depth and guide management and prognosis
Immediate airway assessment is critical, as laryngeal oedema can cause rapid airway compromise requiring early intubation or a surgical airway
Late complications include oesophageal and gastric outlet strictures and an increased long-term risk of oesophageal carcinoma
reference.pathophysiology: Corrosive agents produce tissue destruction on contact. Strong alkalis (e.g. lye, drain cleaner) cause liquefactive necrosis, saponifying fats and dissolving proteins, allowing deep penetration and full-thickness oesophageal injury with risk of perforation and mediastinitis. Strong acids cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation that can limit depth of penetration but tends to pool in and damage the stomach, risking gastric perforation and peritonitis. Injury severity depends on the agent, concentration, volume, and contact time. Healing of deep circumferential burns leads to fibrosis and stricture, and chronic injury raises long-term malignancy risk.
additionalDifferentials: Thermal or scald injury to the upper aerodigestive tract
Acute epiglottitis or other airway infection
Peptic ulcer disease or spontaneous oesophageal perforation
additionalInvestigations: Early upper GI endoscopy to grade mucosal injury
Erect chest and abdominal imaging to detect free air or mediastinal air
CT of the chest and abdomen to assess transmural injury and perforation
Arterial blood gas and lactate as markers of tissue necrosis
Full blood count, electrolytes, and group and save in case surgery is needed
redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness, or respiratory distress indicating airway involvement
Severe chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting oesophageal or gastric perforation
Haemodynamic instability, metabolic acidosis, or rising lactate
Subcutaneous emphysema or free air on imaging
reference.prognosis: Minor mucosal injury usually heals well, but deep circumferential burns commonly progress to strictures needing repeated dilatation or surgery, and full-thickness injury with perforation carries high mortality; survivors have a lifelong increased risk of oesophageal cancer.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal mouth excludes serious oesophageal or gastric damage
Attempting to neutralise the corrosive or induce vomiting, which aggravates injury
Giving activated charcoal, which is ineffective and hinders endoscopy
Delaying airway management in a patient with evolving laryngeal oedema
management: Immediate airway assessment and protection, with early intubation for stridor or laryngeal oedema, and keep the patient nil by mouth
Avoid emesis, neutralising agents, gastric lavage and activated charcoal, all of which worsen tissue injury and obscure endoscopy
Resuscitate with intravenous fluids and provide adequate analgesia
Perform early upper GI endoscopy once stabilised to grade mucosal injury depth and guide management and prognosis
Give a proton pump inhibitor for acid suppression, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics only if perforation or mediastinitis is suspected
Obtain urgent surgical referral for perforation, mediastinitis or peritonitis, with oesophagectomy or gastrectomy as indicated
Treat resulting strictures with repeated endoscopic dilatation, and provide nutritional support during recovery
Enrol survivors of deep injury in long-term endoscopic surveillance for oesophageal carcinoma
